processing: Fully oxidised black tea; step-by-step detail is little published. Expect the usual withering, rolling, oxidation and drying.
harvest_season: Not well documented. Black teas of this kind are typically most valued in spring.
appearance_dry: Not well documented; typically dark strands, with golden tips in finer grades.
appearance_liquor: Typically a clear golden red, as with other Chinese black teas.
taste_profile: Few independent tasting records exist. Chinese black teas of this kind usually lean sweet and gentle, with some honey and malt.

brewing.notes: General advice for fine black tea: keep the water below the boil and the first steeps short.

vintage_note: Little is recorded about how it is sold. As is usual for this class, it is best within a year or two of production.
description:
Badong Hong is a black tea from Badong county in the Three Gorges part of western Hubei, within Enshi prefecture. The name is closely tied to the Zhengshantang company, so it is better understood as a young branded tea than as a long-standing appellation.

Little is documented about how it is made. It should follow the usual black tea method of withering, rolling, oxidation and drying, and the taste should sit near other Hubei blacks: sweet and malty, but that is a guess from the class rather than a fact about this tea.

If you find some, ask who made it and when it was picked, and brew it like any Chinese gongfu black: short steeps, hot water, and see what is there.
history:
Badong promotes itself as a place linked with Shennong and tea, which is local tradition rather than record, and a county official has described dedicated research on Badong tea as almost nonexistent.

The name is sold today by Zhengshantang, the Wuyi company behind Jin Jun Mei, as a black tea from forest tea plants in Badong. When the name first appeared is not documented.
